titulo.texto: Toltec Warrior Sculpture with Coyote Helmet

frase_gancho.texto: A warrior emerging from the snout of a coyote.

puente_narrativo.texto: The Atlas figure carries a mirror of command on its back. Now look at one made into a jewel: a disk covered in small pieces of turquoise, the tezcacuitlapilli.

guion_corto.texto: A human face peers out from the open jaws of a coyote: the man wears the animal as a helmet. He is a warrior of the Coyote order, one of the fraternities that, together with those of the Eagle and the Jaguar, shared the military power of the Toltec state. Dressing this way was not a costume: it was a way of taking on the animal’s qualities, its cunning, its keen hearing, its strength at nightfall. The coyote was associated with Tezcatlipoca, the god of the night, and with Huehuecóyotl, the Old Coyote, who protected the dance. Notice the ear ornaments and how the snout frames the face.

guion_largo.texto:
In this piece, the man and the animal are not separate: they are fused. The human face emerges from the coyote’s jaws as if the beast were giving birth to him, or devouring him, or protecting him. It is hard to know which of the three. And that ambiguity is exactly what the sculptor wanted: that no one could say where the warrior ends and where the coyote begins.

Why a coyote? Because it is an animal that resembles much of what was admired in a good warrior. It is cunning, resilient, hunts in packs, adapts to almost any place, and howls as evening falls. The very word “coyote,” in Spanish and in English, comes from the Nahuatl coyotl. Like chocolate, tomato, avocado, or chili, the coyote is a word borrowed from Nahuatl, a gift from that language to almost the whole world.

In this city there were orders of warriors. Alongside those of the Eagle and the Jaguar, which you saw on the frieze, there was that of the Coyote. Little is known with certainty about how they worked in Tula, but images like this one suggest that their members dressed in helmets and animal skins, and that the disguise was part of their prestige. Later on, in the Mexica Hall, you will see warriors like these: eagles, jaguars, and also an eagle emerging from a helmet.

The coyote had two divine faces. One was Tezcatlipoca, the “Smoking Mirror,” the god of the night and of fate, who in the mural at the entrance was shown as a jaguar. The other was Huehuecóyotl, the “Old Coyote,” a mischievous god who presided over dance, music, and festivity, and who could also be deceitful. Two extremes: solemn darkness and nocturnal laughter. The coyote fits in both.

By now you will have noticed that the coyote has followed you throughout the tour. In the hall of the first inhabitants it appeared as a carved bone more than ten thousand years old. In Teotihuacán, it was painted in procession on the walls of houses. Here it is an emblem of war. And in Texcoco, shortly before the Conquest, a poet king bore its name, Nezahualcóyotl, “hungry coyote.” That is more than ten thousand years of coyote.

Specialists do not agree on who the figure emerging from the snout is. Some link him with Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl, the god of the wind; others, with Huehuecóyotl; others, simply, with a high-ranking warrior who wanted to resemble the animal. The good thing about this ambiguity is that you do not need to choose: the image works on every level.

Now imagine the helmet being worn, at night, in a city without electricity, with torches on the pyramids. A warrior with a coyote’s head looking down at you, with its mouth open, to inspire fear and respect. This is probably how his enemies saw him. More than a uniform, it was a transformation.

That transformation is an idea you will see again and again, even in the halls upstairs, in the dances of today in which people put on deer, jaguar, and coyote masks. The custom of becoming an animal did not disappear: it changed places, from war to festivity.

texto: Look at how the coyote’s snout frames the human face
Imagine the helmet being worn at night: how would you feel watching it approach?

texto.pregunta: Myth: Dressing up as an animal was just a fashion among warriors.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was a way of taking on the animal’s strength and qualities; it is connected to very ancient beliefs about the nahual.
